content: To encourage the early adoption of an intervention, it is essential to establish a multidisciplinary team that includes representatives from all relevant disciplines impacted by the project. This team should also include experts from various clinical settings to provide diverse perspectives. These individuals can act as clinical champions, promoting the intervention and facilitating its spread. When testing the intervention, it is critical to learn about the implementation process. Interventions requiring additional resources, such as equipment, staff, or materials, must be supported by parallel efforts to ensure success. This is often referred to as system change. Implementation goals should be tailored to the specific setting and rely on robust monitoring and feedback mechanisms, as recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO). Feedback from participants at every opportunity is vital to refine the process. Continuous promotion and iteration of program activities, such as reminders and communication, are necessary. Education and training should be tailored to the needs of participating organizations and individuals. Even facilities unable to implement the entire program can make incremental changes, depending on their local safety climate and culture. At the national or state level, leveraging existing communication channels, networks, and relationships is crucial. Presenting the work at existing meetings, disseminating information through professional organizations, and repurposing teams working on other quality improvement projects can help spread the initiative. Sharing information at staff meetings, grand rounds, and within committees is also effective. Developing and supporting clinical champions is another key strategy. A state-level committee with representatives from all relevant disciplines and facility types can guide the work. Offering a variety of program activities and creating materials to guide organizations through implementation steps, while addressing common barriers, is essential. Convening facility champions to share experiences and solve problems collectively can further enhance the process. Providing clinical champions with the necessary resources and time to implement the project is critical. Coaching plays a significant role in supporting implementation. Hospital site visits can provide valuable feedback to organizations. A coaching program leveraging the implementation team and clinical champions can be established, ensuring that coaches are trained in providing constructive feedback. Encouraging incremental change is important, especially for organizations not ready to implement the entire project. Guidance on implementing smaller components or modifying interventions to fit the local context should be provided. Templates and program materials tailored to the specific environment can facilitate this process. Local culture, resources, and prior quality improvement projects should be considered when modifying program materials. A facility-level leadership team can guide the work and allocate resources. Barriers to delivering high-quality, safe care are often similar across health systems. Evidence-based elements that improve processes and practices to prevent surgical site infections (SSIs) have been identified. A multimodal approach is critical for successful SSI prevention. Key barriers and challenges should be addressed to stimulate reflection and action at the local level. The Four E’s model—engage, educate, execute, and evaluate—has been identified as a critical framework for successful improvement programs. This model integrates technical and adaptive (culture change) work to translate evidence into bedside practice. Multiple components of the Four E’s can be implemented simultaneously, depending on the local context. Engagement involves involving all relevant staff to explain the importance of the intervention and achieve buy-in and commitment. A written action plan, endorsed by the multidisciplinary team and facility management, is essential. Regular meetings to identify stakeholder expectations, brainstorm causes and effects, plan implementation, review progress, and measure outcomes are necessary. Tools such as case-based teaching videos, standardized scripts, and structured communication frameworks (e.g., SBAR) can enhance engagement. Education focuses on sharing evidence supporting the interventions with all involved. Training frontline staff on measures to reduce SSIs is crucial. A mix of teaching modalities, including workshops, grand rounds, briefings, posters, handbooks, webinars, and live simulations, can be used. Education should emphasize the rationale and goals of the changes in patient care to prevent SSIs. Focused training on specific clinical processes, such as skin preparation techniques, can improve attention to detail. Execution involves designing an SSI intervention toolkit that addresses barriers, standardizes processes, and incorporates independent checks. Local ownership and adoption are critical, with preventive measures integrated into the clinical workflow. Assigning clear responsibilities, writing procedures for each step, and timely review of execution strategies are essential. Employing specialized professionals or companies can help collect data, identify root causes, propose solutions, and integrate them into practice. Overall, education and training are integral to improvement strategies but must be complemented by other efforts to achieve sustained success. Partnerships between senior management, administrators, and clinical staff are vital to align improvement efforts with organizational priorities, overcome challenges, and foster accountability.
